name: Fatima Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day of music work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I started paid fiddle work after years sewing costumes. I play a junior part in a folk show, record short tunes and help teach two beginners under a senior teacher who is paid to supervise me. I enjoy the moment the dancers catch the beat; I still need that teacher to catch my rough bowing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps that work possible at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner works at the post office and our grown children live elsewhere. We have a mortgage and ten months of expenses saved; the travelling show pays well for a junior player, and other venues are nearby. I have secondary schooling, never use AI tools and check bookings with the show manager by phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the show manager that a quicker booking sheet is welcome if the fiddlers and their rehearsal fees stay on it. I would still check dates by phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our show dates, two paid pupils and my partner’s wage cover the mortgage. Ten months saved gives us room for a cancelled weekend, but I do not know my pension figure yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep the paid show, recordings and two supervised pupils, and request the next run’s written rehearsal fees. In the first plateau year I would request my actual pension estimate before naming a retirement date and save one fifth of cleared extra recording fees after mortgage, food and travel toward twelve months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our pay in this picture. I would rather count signed folk-show dates than talk as though my birthday were a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the senior teacher get paid for those pupils?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the school pays her to supervise the lesson, and I get my junior teaching fee. I would not offer an unsupervised class just to look established.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop touring at a set age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not set one. I need the pension estimate and our actual bills before making a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the show manager whether paid short recordings are being replaced. I would also ask who pays the senior teacher when a beginner lesson is moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the small recording calls to thin and the show may cut a paid rehearsal. Both fees help our mortgage, though ten months saved means we can look for another paid date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the show and two supervised pupils, and get rehearsal and cancellation rates in writing. If two monthly recordings disappear, I would look for a posted paid costume-store assistant role only if my secondary schooling and sewing experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces the lost music fees and the route works; I would keep music until a signed offer and use the same rule during disruption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing fees I count, not about being unable to eat next week. A real vacancy and a written wage matter more than a comforting rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why return to costume work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know stock and cloth from the years I spent sewing, but I would read the actual role. I will not call myself a designer to get a job I cannot do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to remake a fiddle tune?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used it, and I am still practising the tune in my own hands. A rehearsal is where I need help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the show that 2028 thinking AGI could book and make fiddle recordings before robot players arrive around 2031. I would ask for paid dates on paper now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect short recording calls to stop and some paid rehearsals to disappear in 2028. That would be a noticeable cut to my own pay, even with the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would secure written show dates and keep the two supervised pupils. In the first year after 2028, if recordings end and paid rehearsals shrink, I would apply for a posted paid costume-store assistant job only if secondary schooling and sewing experience meet its requirements, written net pay after travel replaces the lost fees and transport works; I would keep paid music until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a fast income cut, but there are other venues and ten months saved. I would not take the costume job on an old memory of what it paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the senior teacher still be involved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, she would be paid to supervise the two beginner lessons while I still teach them. I am not qualified to promise advanced teaching alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the later robot date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Capable robot fiddlers are around 2031 in this card. The booking and recordings can lose buyers in 2028, which is the first fee I would check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell families that five years lets us agree a fair price for beginner fiddle lessons. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031 and robot fiddlers around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recordings may fade, but live beginner playing could last. I would consider a separate basic class only with the senior teacher beside me and paid for her work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the paid show and supervised pupils and get the community hall’s room booking and hire charge in writing before taking any deposits. If two monthly recordings disappear, I would offer a separate basic fiddle class only after eight paid places cover my teaching/preparation, the senior teacher’s supervision wage, room hire, instrument hire and travel; I would inspect each fiddle and replace an unsafe one or defer and refund the whole group if eight safe paid places cannot be maintained, renewing after 2031 only with the same safe floor and full pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about recording fees over the next few years. Five years gives me time to find eight paying families without spending the reserve on a room first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why refund everybody for one broken fiddle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would try a safe replacement first. If I cannot keep eight safe paid places, the class no longer covers the teacher and my preparation, so I would defer and refund the whole group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach without the senior player?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I am still learning and the advertised class would name her paid supervision. I would not swap the senior teacher’s wage for a louder poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot fiddlers around 2039 are different dates. I would ask the show what a paid rehearsal earns today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may play fewer touring dates, but I have no retirement date until the pension estimate is in my hand. Ten months saved and my partner’s wage make the next few years steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep the paid show and two supervised pupils, request my actual pension estimate and save a fifth of cleared extra recording fees after mortgage, food and travel toward twelve months. Over the decade I would run a separate basic fiddle class only after written room booking and hire charge are agreed before deposits; eight deposits pay my teaching/preparation, senior supervision, room hire, safe instrument hire and travel, replacing unsafe fiddles or deferring and refunding the whole group below eight safe paid places; in the first year after 2036 I would renew only while the same full paid floor holds and keep show dates that still pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant recordings, not the next mortgage payment. I need an actual pension figure and paid class seats before I change a working week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the class fiddles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would hire safe instruments only when deposits cover the hire and the reserve stays untouched. A broken one must be replaced or the whole group deferred and refunded below eight safe places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire as soon as a statement arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The figure, bills and health would have to make sense together. A pension statement is a fact to check, not an order to leave music.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because recordings and rehearsals could lose fees before I replace them. Signed show dates, a real qualifying costume-store vacancy and written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a beginner lesson has an experienced teacher watching the bow. I am a paid learner too, and the senior teacher’s hour has to be in the price.

She has **ten months saved**, a postal-working partner, grown children and a mortgage.
She has **never used AI** and teaches beginners only with a paid senior supervisor.
Her **separate class** needs a written room, eight safe paid places and full wages before renewal.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could cut recordings and rehearsal pay before a replacement role appears.
